opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to a gap that a lot of people in China's research community feel but don't always say out loud. Over the past decade we've become very good at the engineering side: taking an idea, scaling it, optimizing it, shipping it. In AI especially, Chinese teams can now match or beat almost anyone on execution. But the truly original questions, the ones that might not pay off for ten or twenty years, still don't have a natural home.

Universities are under pressure to produce papers and rankings. Companies, even the well-funded ones, ultimately have to answer to product cycles and commercial returns. Government funding matters a lot, but it tends to favor projects that are already legible, where you can write down the milestones in advance. Basic research often doesn't work like that. The most important results usually come from someone being allowed to wander, fail for a few years, and follow a hunch nobody else believes in.

A public-interest organization can sit in that space between. It doesn't need to show a profit, and it doesn't need to justify every grant with a five-year plan. It can bet on people rather than projects, especially young researchers who haven't yet built the reputation to get mainstream funding. I think that's where a lot of the hidden talent in China is right now. There are many brilliant people in their twenties who are curious and capable, but the system nudges them toward safe, incremental work.

There's also a cultural reason. In the West, there's a long tradition of foundations, wealthy individuals, and nonprofits funding science purely out of curiosity or a sense of responsibility. In China that tradition is still young. As more people in our industry have done well, I think we have an obligation, and honestly an opportunity, to give some of that back in a way that strengthens the foundation everyone stands on. If we only ever build on top of other people's discoveries, we'll always be following. Supporting basic research is how you eventually get to lead.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention AGI or a competition over who can conduct research faster.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the reason is actually quite simple. In China today, the resources available to do real foundational work are heavily concentrated in a handful of large companies and a few government-backed labs. If you're a young researcher with a genuinely original idea, especially one that won't turn into a product in eighteen months, your options are narrow. You either join a big company and have your agenda shaped by the business, or you stay in academia and spend most of your energy chasing compute and grant cycles.

What I kept noticing while working on large models is that the most important progress often came from directions nobody had a commercial reason to fund at the time. Attention, scaling laws, mixture-of-experts: these started as curiosity-driven questions. If we only fund what already looks like it will pay off, we're essentially outsourcing our research agenda to whoever happens to have the biggest balance sheet right now.

So a public-interest organization fills a specific gap. It can give patient money and real compute to people working on problems with long time horizons, without demanding a return or a roadmap. It can act as a neutral ground where researchers from different companies and universities actually share results instead of guarding them. And it can take bets that are too risky for a quarterly-driven company and too unconventional for a traditional funding committee.

There's also a cultural dimension. I'd like more talented people in China to feel that doing deep, slow, unglamorous research is a respected path, not a consolation prize for failing to get into a hot startup. Institutions shape what people aspire to. If we build one that visibly rewards depth and openness, that changes what the next generation thinks is worth doing.

I don't think this replaces industry or the state. It's complementary. But I believe a healthy research ecosystem needs a third pole, one whose only mandate is that the knowledge gets created and gets shared.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss AGI or describe competition as a contest over who can conduct research faster.

astra-6.text:
I think the value lies in giving researchers more room to pursue important questions whose answers may take a long time to emerge. Basic research is uncertain by nature. If we require every project to promise an immediate application or a measurable return, some worthwhile ideas may never get a chance.

A public-interest organization can complement existing funding by offering patient, flexible support, especially to young researchers and people exploring ideas across disciplines. That could mean giving someone the resources to test an unconventional hypothesis without making them spend most of their time justifying short-term results.

But creating an organization is only a starting point. Its value depends on how it operates: whether it respects scientific judgment, allocates funding fairly, and remains accountable while accepting that some research will fail. For me, the aim would be to create conditions in which researchers can do work that matters, even when we cannot yet predict where it will lead.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes requiring immediate applications or measurable returns, but does not mention demands for a complete product.

r002.rationale: It discusses flexible funding, but says nothing about computing resources or supporting infrastructure systems.

r003.rationale: It does not mention AGI or a shift in competition toward research speed.

sol-6.1.text:
I see the value in giving researchers more room to pursue important questions whose usefulness may not be obvious today. Basic research often takes a long time, and the path to a breakthrough is uncertain. If support depends too heavily on short-term results, some promising ideas may never get a chance.

A public-interest organization can complement existing funding by offering patient, flexible support. In China, that could mean helping young researchers develop independent directions and bringing people from different disciplines together. The aim would be to support the conditions for discovery: time, trust, and the freedom to explore.
